sections.title: 1.1 Definitions of Statistics, Probability, and Key Terms
sections.markdown:
The science of statistics deals with collecting, analyzing, interpreting, and presenting data. Descriptive statistics organizes and summarizes data. Inferential statistics uses probability to draw conclusions from data.

A population is the whole collection under study. A sample is a subset of the population. A statistic describes a sample; a parameter describes the whole population.

Exam scores of 86, 75, and 92 have a mean of 84.3 to one decimal place. In a class of 40 students, 22 men and 18 women give proportions of 22/40 and 18/40.

sections.title: 3.1 Terminology
sections.markdown:
An outcome is a result of an experiment. The sample space is the set of all possible outcomes. An event is a subset of the sample space.

Probabilities lie between 0 and 1 inclusive. Probability 0 means an event never happens; probability 1 means it always happens. Probability 0.5 means it is equally likely to happen or not happen.

Equally likely outcomes have equal probabilities. Each face of a fair six-sided die is equally likely. Heads and tails are equally likely for a fair coin.

sections.title: 3.2 Independent and Mutually Exclusive Events
sections.markdown:
Independent and mutually exclusive do not mean the same thing. For independent events, knowing that one occurred does not change the chance of the other occurring.

A bag contains four blue and three white marbles. Drawing a marble, recording its color, and replacing it leaves the probability of blue at 4/7 on the second draw.

Without replacement, if the first marble drawn is blue, three blue and three white remain. The chance of blue on the second draw is then 3/6, or 1/2. Removing the first marble changes the second-draw probabilities.

sections.title: 4.3 Binomial Distribution (Optional)
sections.markdown:
A binomial experiment has a fixed number n of trials. Each trial has two possible outcomes, called success and failure. The trials are independent and use identical conditions.

The probability of success on a trial is p; the probability of failure is q. These probabilities stay the same on each trial, and p + q = 1. The random variable X counts successes in the n trials.

In an elementary physics course, the withdrawal rate is 30 percent and 70 percent of students stay for the entire term. If X counts students who withdraw, withdrawal is called success. Success names the outcome measured; it need not be a good outcome.

sections.title: 6.1 The Standard Normal Distribution
sections.markdown:
The standard normal distribution has mean 0 and standard deviation 1. A z-score tells how many standard deviations a score lies above or below the mean.

The formula is z = (x - mu) / sigma. Solving for the original score gives x = mu + z * sigma.

For a data set with mean 5 and standard deviation 2, a score of 11 has z-score 3. Scores above the mean have positive z-scores; scores below it have negative z-scores. A score equal to the mean has z-score zero.
